title: The Boat

jokes.text: Angela pulls multiple coworkers aside to confess her affair with the Senator, framing it with gravity and requesting 'sensitivity, maturity, and discretion'
jokes.setup: Angela addresses coworkers with extreme solemnity, as though delivering life-or-death news requiring the utmost discretion
jokes.punchline: The irony is that Angela is asking for maturity and discretion from the Dunder Mifflin office — the absolute worst possible group for that — and she keeps repeating this to multiple people, negating any discretion herself
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-specific: Angela's prim, self-righteous insistence on discretion while doing exactly the indiscreet thing (telling everyone) is perfectly her. The audience familiar with Angela's judgmental personality finds her hypocrisy funny without it being spelled out.

jokes.text: Andy's talking-head about his family's financial meltdown: 'The Nards hurting? Yeah, you bet. Got kicked pretty hard. Family's shattered, supersad. But I'm kind of crushing it in the damage-control department. So, that's cool.'
jokes.setup: Andy describes a genuinely catastrophic family collapse — father fled to Argentina with a younger woman, brother locked in the wine cellar, all money gone
jokes.punchline: Andy's bro-ish self-congratulation ('kind of crushing it') delivered in the same breath as 'family's shattered, supersad' creates a jarring tonal mismatch that's perfectly Andy
jokes.explanation: Andy's emotional obliviousness and performative competence colliding with genuine family tragedy is perfectly on-brand. 'Kind of crushing it in the damage-control department. So, that's cool.' is a pitch-perfect Andy line — the hedged bro-pride undercut by the catastrophe around him.

jokes.text: 'I wish my dad could see me now. Of course, he caused this whole mess, so... [implied expletive] him.'
jokes.setup: Andy expresses a genuine, vulnerable wish that his dad could witness him stepping up
jokes.punchline: He immediately catches himself, remembers his dad IS the cause of all this, trails off with barely-restrained profanity — the emotional whiplash from tender to resentful in two seconds
jokes.explanation: The joke earns its laugh through genuine emotional grounding — Andy's complicated feelings about his father are real, so the snap reversal lands harder. The implied profanity (censored mid-sentence) is funnier than the word itself would be. Good economy and strong character specificity.

jokes.text: Kevin's response to Angela's heartfelt plea: 'That's beautiful. No, I totally get that.'
jokes.setup: Angela delivers an emotional, earnest appeal to Kevin about keeping her affair secret because 'this means the world to me'
jokes.punchline: Kevin responds with sincere-sounding validation ('That's beautiful') that reveals he has absorbed none of the actual content — he's performing understanding without having it
jokes.explanation: Kevin performing emotional intelligence he clearly doesn't have is a reliable but not groundbreaking gag. Works because of his sincerity — he genuinely thinks he's nailing this — but doesn't reach the heights of his 'Why?' line.

jokes.text: 'That's beautiful. No, I totally get that.' — Kevin responds to Angela's desperate secret-keeping plea
jokes.setup: Angela has just begged Kevin to keep her affair secret, saying 'this means the world to me'
jokes.punchline: Kevin responds with warm, genuine-sounding affirmation — 'That's beautiful' — as if he has actually absorbed the emotional weight, but his subsequent behavior proves he hasn't
jokes.explanation: Kevin performing emotional intelligence he clearly doesn't have is a reliable joke in his character's wheelhouse. Works competently, foreshadows his inability to keep the secret.

jokes.text: 'I really want to. Whatever happens, always remember that.' / 'I don't know what that means.'
jokes.setup: Angela presses Kevin on whether he can keep her secret; Kevin gives a cryptic, vaguely philosophical non-answer
jokes.punchline: Angela's exasperated 'I don't know what that means' mirrors the audience's confusion and deflates Kevin's inadvertent profundity
jokes.explanation: Kevin accidentally stumbles into sounding deep while meaning nothing — a solid character beat that works because his sincerity is total. Angela's frustrated literalism is the perfect straight-man reaction.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, she hosts The Dr. Laura Show.' / 'Nope, that's Dr. Laura.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks if anyone knows Iris Black on the radio; a coworker confidently identifies her as the host of The Dr. Laura Show
jokes.punchline: Pam flatly corrects: 'Nope, that's Dr. Laura' — the coworker has essentially defined Iris Black as 'not Iris Black'
jokes.explanation: A quick, economical gag about office-worker confidently wrong knowledge. Functional but not character-specific enough to be memorable.

jokes.text: Dwight bursting forward yelling 'I do! I do! I do I do I do I do!' to volunteer for the radio interview
jokes.setup: Pam asks if anyone feels particularly passionate about local business issues, clearly expecting a measured response
jokes.punchline: Dwight's explosion of enthusiasm — presumably physical, lunging forward — plus the repeated 'I do' like a deranged wedding guest, signals his desperate hunger for recognition and authority
jokes.explanation: Dwight's ambition and grandiosity make this work — nobody else in the office would respond this way. The repetition of 'I do' escalates the absurdity just enough.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking-head fantasy: imagining people saying 'Ten reams of 40-pound bond at only $6.90 after discount? Whatever you say, Brad Pitt!' as proof that fame sells paper
jokes.setup: Dwight reasons that media fame will make it easy to sell paper
jokes.punchline: His imagined dialogue is hilariously specific ($6.90 after discount, 40-pound bond) and the Brad Pitt comparison reveals his completely unexamined self-image
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the paper specs ('ten reams of 40-pound bond at only $6.90 after discount') is brilliant — it grounds Dwight's fantasy in his actual job obsession. Comparing himself to Brad Pitt while discussing paper sales is perfectly absurd and totally in character. The joke only works with Dwight saying it.

jokes.text: Meredith, upon hearing Andy's brother is in rehab, immediately asks 'Which place? The one right near Philly? I could be there in an hour.'
jokes.setup: Andy mentions his brother is in rehab; normal social response would be sympathy
jokes.punchline: Meredith's predatory interest in the rehab facility's location — apparently for romantic pursuit of a vulnerable man in recovery — is shockingly inappropriate and totally in character
jokes.explanation: Meredith's instantly predatory response to a man in rehab is dark, specific, and perfectly character-driven. 'I could be there in an hour' sells the joke — it's not hypothetical interest, it's active planning. Could only be Meredith. The economy is excellent: two lines establish the whole horrifying picture. Approaches the 8.0 anchor level.

jokes.text: 'We're done, Meredith.' — Andy shutting down Meredith's follow-up question about how he's holding up
jokes.setup: After Meredith's predatory rehab inquiry, she pivots to asking Andy how he's holding up, apparently trying to seem caring
jokes.punchline: Andy's flat 'We're done, Meredith.' signals he's done engaging and has zero interest in her sudden concern — the dismissal is the joke
jokes.explanation: A solid button on the Meredith sequence. Economy is strong ('We're done, Meredith' is three words that say everything) but it's the third beat of the gag so it's somewhat diminished.

jokes.text: Dwight doing a tongue twister ('Greta, the tittle-tattle, prattled on about the little metal bottle...') as vocal warm-up for the radio interview, with increasing absurdity
jokes.setup: Dwight has selected himself for a radio interview and is preparing in the office
jokes.punchline: His warm-up is a ludicrous tongue twister delivered with complete seriousness, interrupted mid-flow — 'Tricky Siskel spat a bit of wicked biscuit' — the escalating nonsense and total commitment sells it
jokes.explanation: Dwight's unironic commitment to professional preparation rituals for a local radio interview is perfectly him. 'Tricky Siskel spat a bit of wicked biscuit' is genuinely funny as gibberish he's treating as essential training.

jokes.text: Darryl says 'I worked at a Jiffy Lube' in response to 'Don't you guys have a place where you spent summers and have all those memories?'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to connect with Andy about selling the family boat by asking if everyone has a place full of summer memories
jokes.punchline: Darryl's flat 'I worked at a Jiffy Lube' perfectly deflates Jim's nostalgic upper-class framing — not a complaint, just a statement of fact that underlines the class difference
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and character integration. Darryl's five-word response dismantles Jim's well-meaning but clueless appeal to shared privilege. It's not performed as a joke — Darryl just states it — which makes it hit harder. The class commentary is built into the joke without being preachy. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its precision and character specificity.

jokes.text: Jim's attempt to use Darryl's Jiffy Lube to convince him Andy would feel the same about the boat, and Darryl's immediate rebuttal: 'I would if I owned it and I went broke.'
jokes.setup: Jim says 'I bet you wouldn't sell that Jiffy Lube for all the money in the world, would you, Darryl?' — trying to create an analogy for Andy's emotional attachment to the boat
jokes.punchline: Darryl immediately punctures the sentiment: 'I would if I owned it and I went broke.' — pure pragmatism vs. Jim's romantic idealism
jokes.explanation: This is a callback that pays off the setup even better. Jim walks right into Darryl's logic and Darryl doesn't blink. The joke works on multiple levels: it's funny, it's a perfect character moment for both Jim (naive idealism) and Darryl (grounded pragmatism), and it inadvertently makes a strong practical argument to Andy. Excellent structure.

jokes.text: 'Well, why don't I go and tell Dwight so he can stop being such a complete nipple?'
jokes.setup: The radio interview is cancelled; Jim suggests breaking the news to Dwight
jokes.punchline: 'Complete nipple' as an insult — mild, British-flavored, oddly specific — coming from Jim, who usually deploys dry wit, signals how much Dwight's pompous preparation has worn on him
jokes.explanation: 'Nipple' as an insult is unexpected and specific enough to land. Slightly out of character for Jim (who usually underplays), but the mildness of the insult is part of the joke — it's the most he can muster.

jokes.text: 'He's going to be disappointed. Yes, he is. And you know what? We cannot let that happen.'
jokes.setup: Jim notes Dwight will be disappointed the interview is cancelled
jokes.punchline: Pam's emphatic 'We cannot let that happen' — delivered as though protecting Dwight is a serious mission — subverts the expectation that she'd just tell him the truth. The dramatic framing of Dwight-disappointment-prevention is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the fake-interview plot. Pam's earnestness about protecting Dwight is sweet and slightly funny but not a standout moment.

jokes.text: Erin's talking-head: 'This isn't how I would cheer up just anyone, but it's a girlfriend's job to know her man, and I know Andy. He is seriously juvenile.' / 'He's like 40, though, right?' / 'Oh, no. He couldn't be more than, like, thirties, tops.'
jokes.setup: Erin explains her strategy for cheering up Andy — acknowledging he's juvenile — while the interviewer apparently challenges her characterization
jokes.punchline: Erin's absolute confidence that Andy is 'thirties tops' when he is visibly in his late thirties/early forties is less about the age and more about her complete uncritical devotion to him — she'd believe anything flattering about him
jokes.explanation: Erin's loyal obliviousness is on brand. The joke is compounded by the off-screen questioner's skepticism, which mirrors the audience.

jokes.text: 'Help! My teeth are all messed up in my mouth.' — Andy's watermelon-teeth face, apparently a visual gag with fake teeth/watermelon rind, interrupting the radio interview in the background
jokes.setup: Erin has engineered some kind of juvenile watermelon-teeth gag to cheer Andy up; Dwight is in the middle of a serious radio interview
jokes.punchline: Andy's theatrical 'Help! My teeth are all messed up in my mouth!' — performed as though genuinely alarmed — combined with the visual of watermelon rind teeth is pure silly comedy interrupting the gravitas of Dwight's interview
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the watermelon teeth setup. Works as physical comedy and as a callback. Andy's theatrical alarm about his own prank is in character — he commits to the bit completely.

jokes.text: Angela snapping at Kevin about 1138 forms: 'Well, I don't know why I'm surprised. Literally nothing you could do could surprise me anymore.' / Kevin: 'Oh, really, Angela? That's interesting. Because I do think that I could surprise you.'
jokes.setup: Angela berates Kevin for not ordering forms, dismissing him as predictably useless
jokes.punchline: Kevin — who is sitting on the secret of her affair — ominously suggests he could surprise her. The dramatic irony (we know what he knows) makes this land on multiple levels
jokes.explanation: Strong use of dramatic irony — Kevin's oblivious threat is funnier because the audience knows exactly what the surprise would be. Angela's blissful condescension toward her own secret-keeper is rich. The setup of Angela dismissing Kevin makes his response perfectly timed.

jokes.text: Kevin pretends to have to go to the bathroom to escape the conversation: 'I have to go to the bathroom!'
jokes.setup: Kevin is about to reveal Angela's secret (or at least dangles the threat); realizing he's about to blow it, he needs an exit
jokes.punchline: His cover is screaming 'I HAVE TO GO TO THE BATHROOM!' and running out — absurdly bad as a cover story, hilarious in its desperation
jokes.explanation: The contrast between Kevin's surprisingly decent discretion instinct and his catastrophically bad execution (screaming bathroom) is funny. Works mostly because of the stakes set up by the Angela secret arc.

jokes.text: Angela's talking-head: 'That actually wasn't the worst cover. I'd say at least once a week Kevin runs out of the room shouting that he has to go to the bathroom. So the supply forms are going to be...' [interrupted by Kevin bursting in yelling 'I have to go to the bathroom!' again]
jokes.setup: Angela, in talking-head, grudgingly admits Kevin's bathroom escape wasn't the worst cover — establishing it as a regular occurrence
jokes.punchline: Kevin immediately bursts in and does it again mid-confessional, proving her point and undermining it simultaneously
jokes.explanation: The structure here is excellent: Angela's talking-head inadvertently provides the setup for Kevin to interrupt and become the punchline in real-time. The mockumentary format is exploited perfectly — Kevin destroying the confessional he's being analyzed in is meta and hilarious. The timing of the interruption is the whole joke and it's very well constructed. Strong candidate for standout moment.

jokes.text: 'All I ever wanted to do was sail the damn thing. But Dad wouldn't let me. He said, "You can't be a skipper until you're a man." You know, I'd reach for the wheel and he'd just smack my hand away.'
jokes.setup: Andy reveals why selling the boat is personally painful — he's always dreamed of sailing it
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'smack my hand away' — casual paternal dismissal — reframes the whole family dynamic as both genuinely sad and darkly funny. Andy's dad casually crushing him is the quiet punchline.
jokes.explanation: More cringe-comedy than pure joke — Andy's father's casual cruelty delivered as ordinary backstory is quietly devastating and funny in a dark way. Sets up the emotional arc of the episode's B-plot.

jokes.text: Dwight's radio interview claim: 'David Wallace is the CEO, but he's not hands-on. So the day-to-day operations are entirely under your command?' / 'Entirely is the perfect way to describe it, Iris.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is on live radio for what appears to be a softball local business interview
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately begins vastly overstating his own authority — 'entirely' is his word of choice, not even trying to be accurate — setting up the escalating catastrophe to come
jokes.explanation: Dwight's grandiosity and self-promotion are his defining traits; claiming total command of Dunder Mifflin on live radio is perfectly Dwight. Functions as setup for the disaster to follow.

jokes.text: Radio producer asks Dwight to remove his shirt because his buttons are causing a clinking sound
jokes.setup: The radio interview begins; there's supposedly a technical issue with audio interference from Dwight's shirt buttons
jokes.punchline: The request to remove his shirt entirely (rather than, say, move the microphone) is the beginning of an absurd escalation of requests designed to humiliate Dwight, who complies without suspicion
jokes.explanation: The shirt request launches the escalating prank — Pam and Jim are running a fake interview to spare Dwight's feelings, and the absurdity of the requests is the engine of the joke. Dwight's lack of suspicion is the core of the comedy.

jokes.text: Radio producer claims Dwight's voice sounds 'a little feminine' and asks if he's wearing pants with a metallic zipper — implying he should remove his pants too
jokes.setup: Dwight has already removed his shirt for the 'interview'; the prank escalates
jokes.punchline: 'Your voice, it's sounding a little feminine.' / 'That's impossible.' — Dwight's affronted dignity at having his masculinity questioned is funnier than the request itself. The pants follow logically in the escalation.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from shirt to pants is well-paced and Dwight's 'That's impossible' — his reflex defense of his own manliness — is perfectly in character and very quotable. The meta-joke is that Pam and Jim are essentially hazing Dwight out of his clothes while pretending to protect him.

jokes.text: Angela's conversation about Senator Lipton: 'Last night he was so tired, he just wanted a little Mexican brought in.' Oscar reacts with horrified restraint: 'I can't! It's too much!'
jokes.setup: Angela is innocently describing her husband the Senator's evening — he wanted Mexican food delivered. Oscar, who is having an affair WITH the Senator, hears every innocent statement as a double entendre about their relationship.
jokes.punchline: Oscar's 'I can't! It's too much!' — desperate, barely-contained — while Angela remains completely oblivious, is the peak of dramatic irony. 'A little Mexican brought in' reads entirely differently to Oscar.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's richest comedic vein. Angela's innocent description of her husband wanting 'a little Mexican brought in' is perfectly constructed to land as accidental innuendo given that Oscar (who is Mexican-American) is sleeping with the Senator. The triple-layered dramatic irony — Angela doesn't know about Oscar, Oscar knows about Angela, the audience knows about both — makes Oscar's tortured restraint exponentially funnier. Excellent character integration: this joke only exists because of the specific identity of these three characters and their specific relationships. Among the episode's best.

jokes.text: 'The Senator is just pushing back as hard as he can.' — Oscar's cringe reaction: 'Hmm! Please stop!'
jokes.setup: Angela continues describing her husband's political campaign using physically suggestive language
jokes.punchline: Oscar's involuntary 'Hmm!' followed by desperate 'Please stop!' continues the escalating torment — each innocent phrase is further ammunition
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Angela's accidentally suggestive language and Oscar's increasingly desperate reactions is the episode's strongest running gag. Each iteration lands harder because Oscar's composure is more visibly crumbling.

jokes.text: Oscar's talking-head: 'I'm in big trouble.' / Documentary narrator voice-over: 'Yeah, Oscar's in big trouble.'
jokes.setup: Oscar has just barely survived Angela's innocent innuendo barrage
jokes.punchline: Oscar's deadpan 'I'm in big trouble' is an understatement of the year — confirmed by the show's own narrator echoing him, which is a rare moment of the documentary frame commenting on itself
jokes.explanation: The narrator's deadpan echo of Oscar ('Yeah, Oscar's in big trouble') is an unusual meta moment for The Office's documentary format. Simple and effective — the understatement works because we've just witnessed exactly how much trouble he's in.

jokes.text: Dwight on live radio: 'This is gotcha journalism. But you know what? They're not gonna gotch me.'
jokes.setup: Iris reveals the Consumer Product Safety Commission claims Dunder Mifflin paper is toxic — an ambush interview
jokes.punchline: 'They're not gonna gotch me' — Dwight's invented backformation of 'gotcha' into a verb ('gotch') is a malapropism that reveals his bluster while trying to sound commanding
jokes.explanation: 'They're not gonna gotch me' is a genuinely funny line — the invented verb 'gotch' sounds confident while revealing Dwight doesn't quite grasp the phrase he's using. Good economy and very quotable.

jokes.text: Sondra Mick ambush: 'Is your paper toxic?' / 'No. The paper's not toxic.' / 'Thank you, Sondra!' / '...Unless it's exposed to oxygen. Then it becomes extremely toxic.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is relieved when his own mill foreman Sondra Mick appears to confirm the paper isn't toxic
jokes.punchline: 'Unless it's exposed to oxygen. Then it becomes extremely toxic.' — the devastating qualifier arrives just after Dwight has celebrated, describing a paper that is toxic in literally all conditions of use
jokes.explanation: Structurally one of the best jokes in the episode. The false reassurance ('No, the paper's not toxic') followed by Dwight's premature 'Thank you, Sondra!' is perfectly timed — and then the qualifier 'unless it's exposed to oxygen' is the devastating kicker. The logic is absurdist (paper that becomes toxic when exposed to oxygen is unusable paper) but delivered with complete deadpan conviction. High quotability. The structure mirrors a 9.0 anchor-level design.

jokes.text: Dwight's stock-price-plummeting chaos: 'Get out of here, moron!' to David Wallace, then realizing he's on air: 'Uh... No one. Did you just call Ms. Mick a moron?'
jokes.setup: Dwight is simultaneously managing the live radio disaster and an off-air call from the CEO; he snaps at Wallace
jokes.punchline: Iris catches him calling someone a moron on air — Dwight's scramble to deny it while clearly having just done it, combined with the misattribution (she thinks he called her guest a moron), creates cascading chaos
jokes.explanation: The escalating chaos of Dwight managing too many crises simultaneously is classic farce. His reflex cruelty to Wallace and the immediate on-air exposure is well-paced.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking-head: 'Hey, Oscar, what if I'm getting a promotion? I hope that's it, Kevin. Me, too. 'Cause then I would get my own office. And I wouldn't screw up your secret with Angela. I've been really worried about that.'
jokes.setup: Kevin speculates about why he's being called in; Oscar plays along hoping it's a promotion
jokes.punchline: Kevin's reason for wanting the promotion — so he'd have his own office and thus be less likely to accidentally reveal Angela's secret — is a perfect Kevin logic chain: self-interested, misguided, but accidentally revealing more than he intends
jokes.explanation: Kevin's logic is delightfully Kevin: he wants a promotion primarily because spatial separation would reduce his own liability for secret-keeping failure. It's selfish, oblivious, and accidentally transparent about how badly he's been managing the secret. Good dramatic irony with Oscar, who has his own secret.

jokes.text: Oscar bribing Kevin with snack machine money to separate Kevin from Angela mid-conversation
jokes.setup: Oscar sees Kevin about to say something to Angela that will blow the affair secret; he needs to extract Kevin immediately
jokes.punchline: 'Snack machine, on me.' — Oscar's desperate bribe works instantly, and Kevin's 'That is nice. Classy move.' is a perfect reaction that misses the obvious manipulation entirely
jokes.explanation: Kevin calling Oscar's transparent bribe 'classy' is the joke — Kevin's sincere admiration of manipulation he's the victim of is character-perfect. Oscar's desperation and Kevin's unsuspecting gluttony work beautifully together.

jokes.text: Oscar confessing to Dwight he made up the gambling accusation against Kevin: 'Those figures I gave you? They're false. No. I was mad at Kevin. We had a fight, and I acted vindictively.'
jokes.setup: Dwight had sent Kevin home based on Oscar's false accusation of a gambling relapse
jokes.punchline: Dwight's response: 'I knew it. I knew it from the beginning this was a possibility.' — Dwight claiming to have anticipated the false accusation despite having completely believed it, retroactively rewriting his own gullibility as prescience
jokes.explanation: Dwight's retroactive claim of prescience is a great character beat — his ego cannot admit he was fooled, so he instantly rewrites history. Oscar's 'What are you talking about? I just did this now.' perfectly calls it out.

jokes.text: Dwight's Scranton Strangler digression: 'A few years ago, when I was on the jury, the Scranton Strangler? I always thought he might have been set up, but I felt pressured to convict.' / 'Well, that's got to be tough.' / 'Tough? I put an innocent man on death row.'
jokes.setup: Dwight uses the Kevin false-accusation situation as a trigger for his anxieties about the Scranton Strangler conviction
jokes.punchline: Dwight's absolute conviction that he may have helped execute an innocent man — delivered mid-scene as a detour — is darkly funny both as absurdist non-sequitur and as a callback to the series-long Scranton Strangler running gag. 'I put an innocent man on death row' as a casually dropped statement.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's guilt about the Scranton Strangler is a long-running Office bit that rewards loyal viewers. The casual delivery of 'I put an innocent man on death row' mid-conversation about office drama is perfectly calibrated dark comedy. Works as both a standalone non-sequitur and a series callback.

jokes.text: News radio report: 'Since Mr. Dwight Schrute began speaking, Dunder Mifflin share prices fell 73%.'
jokes.setup: Dwight's radio interview has been a cascading disaster; we now get an external metric of the damage
jokes.punchline: 73% stock drop directly attributed to Dwight speaking — a specific, authoritative number that makes the absurdity concrete and official
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '73%' is the joke — not a round number, not 'plummeted,' but a precise figure that makes the disaster feel real and measured. Good escalation of the radio plot.

jokes.text: Andy's first look at the family boat: 'Oh, my gosh, Andy! This is enormous!' / 'I thought it was going to be tiny!'
jokes.setup: Andy has described the family boat with emotional attachment; Erin expected something modest given the family's financial collapse
jokes.punchline: Erin's delighted surprise that it's actually enormous — 'I thought it was going to be tiny!' — recontextualizes the family's apparent poverty as selective (they spent money on a massive sailboat)
jokes.explanation: A pleasant character reaction but not a strong joke. Erin's delight is in character but the observation isn't sharp enough to be memorable.

jokes.text: 'So this is how your family came to America.' — Erin to Andy about the enormous sailboat
jokes.setup: Erin and Andy arrive at the large family sailboat; Erin is processing the scale of it
jokes.punchline: Erin's earnest suggestion that the boat was used for immigration — completely misreading Andy's WASPy rich family — is innocent and absurd. She has no context for what a leisure yacht signifies vs. an immigrant ship.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's better character-comedy lines. Erin's guileless misreading of an obvious leisure boat as an immigration vessel perfectly encapsulates her social naivety while being genuinely clever. Strong economy and excellent character integration — only Erin could say this without irony.

jokes.text: The captain rebuking Andy: 'I'm not a ghost, so I can't walk through people.' / Erin: 'He was salty.' / Andy: 'He is, a little bit.'
jokes.setup: The boat captain briskly dismisses Andy's sentimental hovering; Andy gets in his way
jokes.punchline: The captain's literal reason for needing Andy to move — 'I'm not a ghost, so I can't walk through people' — is a perfectly deadpan non-joke delivered as though it's profound. Erin's 'He was salty' and Andy's 'He is, a little bit' button it perfectly.
jokes.explanation: The captain's logic is unassailable and delivered entirely without humor, which makes it funny. Erin's straight-faced maritime pun ('salty') and Andy's unaware confirmation make a nice three-beat sequence.

jokes.text: 'Damn it! Screw you, Dad!' — Andy, after being denied permission to touch anything on the boat, alone on the dock
jokes.setup: Andy has been repeatedly denied any interaction with the boat he's selling; his father's ghost of dismissal haunts every moment
jokes.punchline: 'Damn it! Screw you, Dad!' — directed at an absent man who can't hear him, for a situation entirely of that man's making, is both genuinely funny and genuinely sad. The outburst is disproportionate and yet perfectly proportionate.
jokes.explanation: Andy's outburst is cathartic comedy that works because it's been earned. The callback to his father physically preventing him from sailing, combined with the captain's physical prevention, makes 'Screw you, Dad!' justified and funny. The 'Huh.' reaction (presumably from Erin) buttons it perfectly.

jokes.text: 'Well, we're doing it. We're finally having a picnic on the boat!' — Erin, cheerfully reframing the failed sailing attempt as a success
jokes.setup: Andy wanted desperately to sail the boat; he's been denied at every turn
jokes.punchline: Erin enthusiastically reframes sitting on a docked boat eating sandwiches as achieving the goal — her relentless positivity is either oblivious or deeply kind, and it's funny either way
jokes.explanation: Erin's positive reframing is sweet and characterful. The gap between what she says ('we're doing it!') and what's actually happening (they're sitting on a docked boat) is the joke.

jokes.text: 'Andy, you never had to sail the boat to be a man.' / 'Fine, but I could have.'
jokes.setup: Erin offers Andy a sincere pep talk about his worth not depending on sailing ability
jokes.punchline: Andy's response — not gratitude, not emotional breakthrough, but 'Fine, but I could have.' — is petulant, childish, and absolutely perfect. He accepts the comfort while insisting on the hypothetical.
jokes.explanation: Five words that perfectly encapsulate Andy's character — emotionally stunted, proud, childlike. 'Fine, but I could have.' accepts the premise while refusing to let go of the hypothetical achievement. It's simultaneously a punchline, a character revelation, and oddly relatable. High quotability. Only Andy Bernard says this exact thing. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in precision and character specificity.

jokes.text: Andy declares himself captain: 'I'm the captain.' — three times, with increasing conviction
jokes.setup: Erin has told Andy that as far as she's concerned, he's the captain of the boat
jokes.punchline: Andy repeats 'I'm the captain' with growing conviction, the third time to himself, as if persuading himself — comedic repetition as a character study in Andy needing external validation
jokes.explanation: Good Andy character beat — the repetition reveals his deep need to hear himself say it. Works as escalation comedy with a character truth underneath.

jokes.text: 'How much for that cool fisherman's sweater?' — Andy trying to buy the captain's sweater as he announces he's sailing the boat to the Bahamas himself
jokes.setup: Andy has just announced he's taking the boat to the Bahamas himself — a dramatic, momentous decision
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to negotiating for the captain's sweater — the juxtaposition of the grand gesture with the petty acquisition is perfectly Andy. He wants the costume of adventure as much as the adventure itself.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent joke. Andy's big heroic moment is immediately undercut by his desire for the aesthetic trappings of the role. 'Cool fisherman's sweater' is specific enough to be hilarious and it reveals his character — he's always been about performing competence more than having it. Comparable to 8.0 anchor territory.

jokes.text: Erin asks the sailor: 'How much for that cool fisherman's sweater?'
jokes.setup: Andy has just dramatically announced he's sailing the boat to the Bahamas
jokes.punchline: Erin, in the middle of this dramatic moment, fixates on buying the sailor's sweater — completely unaware of or unbothered by the emotional weight of the scene
jokes.explanation: Erin's total tonal disconnect from the emotional climax is very her. 'Cool fisherman's sweater' mid-dramatic-reveal is a good deflation beat. Character-specific and well-timed.

jokes.text: News radio: 'For those just joining us, terror in Greenwich, where the police have surrounded the house of Dunder Mifflin CEO David Wallace. Wallace is said to be despondent over the company's stock plummet and has taken a mailman hostage.'
jokes.setup: Dwight's radio interview has caused a stock crash; we now check in on the CEO
jokes.punchline: David Wallace has taken a mailman hostage — a completely absurd escalation from 'stock went down' to 'CEO has snapped and is holding postal workers captive'. The specificity of 'a mailman' is the detail that makes it.
jokes.explanation: The Wallace-takes-a-mailman-hostage escalation is delightfully absurd. Wallace is a recurring character with established dignity; seeing him reduced to a hostage crisis over paper company stocks is darkly funny. 'A mailman' as the victim — not a rival, not an employee, just an innocent postal worker — is the perfect arbitrary choice.

jokes.text: 'Please, sir, spare him! Please!' — someone (possibly Dwight) pleading for the mailman's life on air
jokes.setup: Wallace has taken a mailman hostage according to the fake news broadcast
jokes.punchline: Dwight's genuine anguish on behalf of the mailman — treating the fake news scenario as completely real — is Dwight at his most earnestly absurd
jokes.explanation: Works as a straight reaction to the absurdist premise. Dwight's sincerity elevates what could be a generic exclamation into a character beat.

jokes.text: Dwight offering to conference in Wallace during an active police hostage standoff: 'I know Wallace's phone number! Everyone hold, I'll conference him in!'
jokes.setup: Police are managing a hostage situation involving the CEO; Dwight, on live radio, sees this as a problem he can solve with his rolodex
jokes.punchline: Dwight's complete confidence that knowing a phone number is the solution to a hostage standoff — and his cheerful offer to 'conference him in' as though this is a business call — is peak Dwight problem-solving
jokes.explanation: Dwight's confidence in organizational hierarchy solutions to extralegal emergencies is perfectly him. 'I'll conference him in' applied to a hostage crisis is absurd in the most Dwight way possible.

jokes.text: Andy finds his brother Walt in the wine cellar: 'I was having a little trouble with this door, uh, yesterday. I, uh... I think it was yesterday.'
jokes.setup: Andy has discovered his brother Walt has been locked in the wine cellar; Walt was said to be in rehab
jokes.punchline: Walt's vague, blurry uncertainty about how long he's been in there — 'I think it was yesterday' — suggests he's been drinking the wine cellar and has lost track of time. The understatement is the whole joke.
jokes.explanation: The delivery of 'I think it was yesterday' as Walt's best guess about his own imprisonment in a wine cellar is darkly funny. The vagueness implies a level of inebriation that makes the timeline uncertain.

jokes.text: 'I thought you were in rehab.' / 'Yeah, I just, uh... I figured I'd get that first relapse out of the way.'
jokes.setup: Andy is surprised to find his brother, who was supposed to be in rehab, in the wine cellar
jokes.punchline: 'I figured I'd get that first relapse out of the way' — delivered as though this is a reasonable preemptive strategy, as though relapse is a task to check off before rehabilitation begins
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The logic of 'getting the first relapse out of the way' before rehabilitation is darkly brilliant — it treats relapse as an inevitable administrative step rather than a failure, delivered with complete deadpan confidence. High originality, perfect economy, deeply quotable. The joke works because it sounds almost reasonable before the full absurdity lands. This is the episode's closest approach to a standout anchor-level line.

jokes.text: Dwight calls Wallace mid-hostage standoff: 'David, is that you? Oh, thank God! I believe in you. I really do, and I believe in your ability to make the right choices. But David, listen to me carefully. I'm going to need you to let the mailman go, okay?'
jokes.setup: Dwight has conferenced in Wallace during a live hostage standoff; he's now negotiating
jokes.punchline: Dwight's crisis negotiation style — opening with affirmations ('I believe in you!') before pivoting to 'let the mailman go' — is both absurd and strangely touching. The specific 'let the mailman go' is funny because it normalizes the surreal situation.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's mix of genuine warmth ('I believe in you') and crisis negotiator ('let the mailman go') is perfectly him — he manages absurd situations with total seriousness. The affirmation-before-demand structure is a good comedy construction.

jokes.text: 'Dunder Mifflin will be in good hands while you're away in prison.' — Dwight to Wallace
jokes.setup: Dwight has been reassuring Wallace during the hostage standoff; he caps his crisis negotiation with a parting thought
jokes.punchline: 'While you're away in prison' is delivered as a natural closing reassurance — as though prison is just a scheduled absence that needs coverage, like a vacation. Dwight's matter-of-factness about his boss going to prison is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: 'While you're away in prison' is a brilliant piece of character comedy — Dwight's complete lack of moral alarm about his boss's impending incarceration, combined with the sincere offer of coverage, is perfectly Dwight. The economy is excellent: the whole joke lives in that one phrase. Strong candidate for episode highlight.

jokes.text: Wallace: 'Dwight? I'm going to ask you to not call me on my cell anymore. Gotta go.' — hanging up during a live hostage standoff
jokes.setup: Dwight has just told Wallace the company will be fine while he's 'away in prison'; Wallace has presumably been handling an actual hostage situation
jokes.punchline: Wallace's polite but firm 'I'm going to ask you to not call me on my cell anymore. Gotta go.' — as though this is a minor social inconvenience rather than a hostage crisis call — is brilliant deadpan. His priority is blocking Dwight's number.
jokes.explanation: Wallace's polite request to never be called again — delivered mid-hostage-crisis with the same tone as declining a social invitation — is excellent comedy. The 'Gotta go' is the perfect button. The joke requires Wallace's established straight-man dignity to land, and it does. Among the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: Wallace: 'Okay. Dwight? I'm going to ask you to not call me on my cell anymore. Gotta go.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just told his CEO to surrender to the police and assured him the company will be fine without him, on live radio
jokes.punchline: Wallace's response is the perfectly calibrated 'I'm going to ask you to not call me on my cell anymore' — an extraordinarily measured response to an extraordinary situation, treating the whole thing as a minor inconvenience
jokes.explanation: Wallace's response is a masterpiece of understatement — after everything that has happened, his only request is 'don't call my cell.' The 'Gotta go' button is perfect. This is the kind of reaction beat that makes The Office great: the most understated possible response to the most over-the-top situation.

jokes.text: Office erupts into 'Schrute! Schrute! Schrute!' chant after the radio catastrophe
jokes.setup: Dwight has caused a 73% stock crash, a CEO hostage situation, and various other disasters through his radio interview
jokes.punchline: The office cheers for him as though he's a sports hero — they've apparently been entertained, not damaged, by the chaos. Dwight accepts it with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A crowd-pleasing button on the radio plot. Not structurally sophisticated but delivers the emotional payoff audiences want — Dwight gets his moment of glory after unintentionally causing chaos.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking-head: 'Overall, I'd say my first radio interview went pretty much the way I expected.'
jokes.setup: Dwight's radio interview caused a stock crash, a CEO hostage crisis, his own humiliation, and office chaos
jokes.punchline: His calm assessment that it 'went pretty much the way I expected' — with zero self-awareness — is the perfect button on the entire arc. Dwight's self-evaluation system is completely disconnected from reality.
jokes.explanation: The perfect cap on the radio plot. Dwight's total self-satisfaction after a catastrophic performance is his defining character trait weaponized as a punchline. The simplicity and economy of the line make it a strong standout. Comparable to 8.0 anchor territory.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking-head reveal: 'Well, Oscar, I did not get the promotion. He just wanted to update my personal information.' / Angela: 'Why on Earth would you think you were getting a promotion?' / Kevin: 'You know what, Angela? I... Oh, my God!'
jokes.setup: Kevin was hoping for a promotion that would let him move offices and avoid accidentally revealing Angela's secret; it was just a personal info update
jokes.punchline: Kevin is about to use this disappointment as the trigger to reveal Angela's secret ('You know what, Angela? I...') — and cuts himself off with 'Oh, my God!' as he catches himself — the near-miss is the joke, and we know exactly what he almost said
jokes.explanation: The near-miss confession is well-constructed tension comedy. Kevin's 'Oh, my God!' self-interruption is funnier because we know exactly what he almost said. The callback to Kevin's secret-keeping anxiety pays off.

jokes.text: Senator Lipton's arrival: 'Honey! What are you doing here?' / Senator (to Oscar): 'Oscar! Looking very healthy. Getting lots of vigorous exercise?'
jokes.setup: The Senator arrives to surprise Angela; Oscar is present
jokes.punchline: The Senator's knowing comment to Oscar about being 'very healthy' and 'getting lots of vigorous exercise' — code for their affair — in front of an oblivious Angela is peak dramatic irony. The Senator is apparently comfortable enough to flirt with Oscar in front of his wife.
jokes.explanation: The Senator's in-person version of Angela's innocent innuendo is even more cringe-inducing because he's doing it intentionally, in front of his wife. 'Getting lots of vigorous exercise?' is deployed with full awareness of its meaning. Angela's obliviousness and Oscar's horror create a perfectly uncomfortable triangle. Excellent character integration.

jokes.text: 'Oscar! Looking very healthy. Getting lots of vigorous exercise?'
jokes.setup: The Senator greets Oscar in front of Angela and the whole office
jokes.punchline: 'Getting lots of vigorous exercise?' — an extremely loaded question from a man who is having an affair with Oscar, delivered in front of Oscar's wife (Angela), with the Senator's cheery obliviousness or brazenness making it devastating
jokes.explanation: This is the best cringe joke in the episode and one of the strongest in The Office's later seasons. The construction is perfect: the Senator asking Oscar about 'vigorous exercise' in front of Angela, Kevin, and the whole office — it's maximally loaded with dramatic irony because every possible interpretation of his question is incriminating. Angela can't catch it. Oscar is devastated. The audience sees all three layers. The character integration is extremely high — only this senator, with this specific relationship to both Angela and Oscar, can make this line land with this weight.

jokes.text: Oscar's pivot to campaigning: 'We're not just going to sit here and ignore the obvious. Senator Lipton has a big election next week. We all need to give him our support!'
jokes.setup: Angela and Oscar are in an extremely tense moment; Oscar needs to redirect the conversation away from his panic
jokes.punchline: Oscar pivots from near-discovery to enthusiastic campaign boosterism — an absurd subject change that somehow works — and the office breaks into 'USA! USA!' chants, completely swallowing the distraction
jokes.explanation: Oscar's desperate pivot to election boosterism for the man he's sleeping with, in front of the man's wife, while the office chants 'USA!', is a densely layered cringe comedy moment. The absurd escalation (from cover story to office rally) is excellent, and Oscar's relief/guilt is implicit throughout.

jokes.text: Oscar's pivot: 'Senator Lipton has a big election next week... We all need to give him our support!' — becomes a USA chant
jokes.setup: Oscar has just nearly blurted out the affair; he pivots to enthusiastic campaign support
jokes.punchline: The office spontaneously erupts in 'USA! USA!' chanting — a completely disproportionate response to paper company employees supporting a local politician
jokes.explanation: The 'USA' chant is a funny absurdist escalation — Oscar's desperate pivot gets weirdly patriotic support. The joke is partly that it works, and everyone including the Senator enjoys it without realizing why Oscar needed it.

jokes.text: Oscar's talking-head: 'I have to say, I'm impressed with Kevin. He showed a lot of self-control. I totally forgot about the affair for a minute.'
jokes.setup: Oscar has just survived the most cringe-inducing sequence of the episode thanks to Kevin's distraction and the USA chant
jokes.punchline: 'I totally forgot about the affair for a minute.' — Oscar crediting Kevin for causing him to briefly forget his own affair, which is the source of all his stress, is a perfectly absurd statement of relief
jokes.explanation: Oscar's confession that he 'totally forgot about the affair for a minute' — as though that's a relief rather than indicating the depth of his stress — is a great character beat. It lands because the preceding sequence was so intense.

jokes.text: Oscar's second talking-head: 'Oscar is having sex with the Senator and Angela doesn't even know. Her life is a complete sham!'
jokes.setup: Oscar, having just survived a near-miss, gives a talking-head confessional
jokes.punchline: Oscar talks about himself in the third person ('Oscar is having sex with the Senator') and describes Angela's unwitting situation as 'her life is a complete sham!' — with what sounds almost like gossip rather than guilt. The detached third-person framing of his own affair is bizarre and funny.
jokes.explanation: Oscar's third-person confession is a great structural choice — he's describing his own situation with the detachment of a gossip, which reveals the compartmentalization required to live this double life. 'Her life is a complete sham!' is darkly funny delivered by the person making it a sham.

jokes.text: 'Damn it, I'm happy!' — Andy shouting from the boat as it departs
jokes.setup: Andy has decided to sail the boat to the Bahamas himself, with his brother as crew — a genuine emotional breakthrough
jokes.punchline: 'Damn it, I'm happy!' — the expletive-prefaced happiness suggests Andy is surprised and slightly resentful about the happiness, as though it's arrived against his will. The delivery undercuts the sentimentality perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Four words that are perfect Andy: the profanity, the surprise at his own happiness, the slightly aggressive delivery of a positive emotion. It's funny and oddly moving at the same time. Only Andy says this and means it. High economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Damn it, I'm happy!'
jokes.setup: Andy is sailing the boat to the Bahamas with his brother, fulfilling his lifelong dream
jokes.punchline: 'Damn it, I'm happy!' — the frustration in his phrasing is the joke: he's so surprised by happiness that he expresses it with the same energy as anger
jokes.explanation: Four words, and they're the emotional climax of Andy's storyline in this episode. 'Damn it, I'm happy' perfectly captures the character — he's been so trained to suppress emotions and deal with disappointment that genuine happiness comes out in the same register as frustration. Highly quotable, emotionally resonant, and purely Andy.

jokes.text: Erin's talking-head: 'Would I have gone with him if he'd asked me? On his sailboat cruise to the Caribbean? Yes. I think that would have been really fun and romantic.'
jokes.setup: Erin has just helped Andy orchestrate his sailing adventure and sent him off happily
jokes.punchline: Erin's completely matter-of-fact acknowledgment that she would have gone if asked — stated with no bitterness, just honest observation — is funny because it reveals she's more adventurous than Andy assumed, and slightly regretful without performing regret
jokes.explanation: Erin's honest admission is quietly funny — she's not upset, just noting a missed opportunity with the same pragmatism Darryl showed earlier. Good character moment, not a standout joke.

jokes.text: Andy discovering Walt has been hiding in the boat's cabin: 'Hey, bro! It was here all along! No way!' / 'Way!'
jokes.setup: Walt was supposed to be joining Andy as crew; his location on the boat was unclear
jokes.punchline: Walt has been hiding in the cabin — apparently the entire time, perhaps still drinking. The 'No way!' / 'Way!' exchange between two adult men in a crisis situation is simultaneously childlike and sweet.
jokes.explanation: A sweet moment that works more as warm character resolution than a sharp joke. The 'No way!' / 'Way!' callback to Wayne's World-era slang from two grown men in crisis is mildly funny.

jokes.text: 'Erin, I gotta go! Them's my chords!' — Andy noticing his guitar on the boat and switching from emotional goodbye to music
jokes.setup: Andy is in the middle of a tender farewell with Erin
jokes.punchline: 'Them's my chords!' — Andy's abrupt pivot from genuine emotion to delighted guitar ownership, using the archaism 'Them's', is perfectly Andy. He can't sustain a sincere moment without being derailed by something shiny.
jokes.explanation: 'Them's my chords!' is genuinely excellent — the archaic plural possessive combined with Andy's immediate emotional derailment from a tender goodbye is pitch-perfect character comedy. The phrase itself is inherently funny; the context makes it better. Strong economy, maximum character integration. Comparable to 8.0 anchor territory.

jokes.text: Jim's friend 'Flipper': 'You might get to meet my friend Flipper.' / 'Does he have a flipper?' / 'Nope. He, uh... He flipped a table one time when he was drunk.'
jokes.setup: Jim invites Pam to Poor Richard's and mentions his friend Flipper — the name implies a physical deformity
jokes.punchline: Pam's sincere question 'Does he have a flipper?' followed by Jim's explanation that it's because he flipped a table while drunk — subverting the setup completely but with an anticlimactic origin story
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection structure: the name implies physical comedy, the reality is disappointingly mundane (and also sort of alarming — he flipped a table while drunk). Pam's earnest question sells the setup, and Jim's 'He sounds like an idiot' / 'Yeah, he is' button is a nice tag.

jokes.text: 'He sounds like an idiot.' / 'Yeah, he is.' — Pam and Jim's reaction to Flipper
jokes.setup: Jim has explained that Flipper's nickname comes from drunkenly flipping a table
jokes.punchline: Pam's dry verdict ('He sounds like an idiot') and Jim's immediate cheerful agreement ('Yeah, he is') — and yet Jim is still inviting Pam to meet this person — is a perfect little character beat about the friendships people maintain despite knowing better
jokes.explanation: The tag to the Flipper joke works because Jim's cheerful 'Yeah, he is.' contains no defensiveness — he agrees completely and still wants to introduce them. The implicit joke is that Jim has inexplicably maintained this friendship anyway.

tmdb_overview: Money problems plague Andy's family. Meanwhile, Dwight guests on a local radio show, so the staffers harass him with outrageous phone calls, and Kevin unearths a big secret about Oscar.
